title: Library management
scopeHtml: Scope: Books vs copies, loans, fines, reservations, concurrent checkout.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design a library management system: members search books, borrow copies, return them (with a fine if late), and reserve a title when all copies are out.

Clarify: one library or a branch network? Are there multiple copies of one title (yes)? Loan period (14 days), per-member limit (3), fine rate (2 per day)? Reservation queue (first come first served)? Who uses it: members only, or librarians too? (Here: one library, books vs copies, limit 3, 14 days, fine per day, FIFO waitlist with notification.)

Worked example. "Clean Code" has 1 copy. Asha borrows it on 1 Jan, due 15 Jan. Ravi reserves it. Asha returns it on 21 Jan: 6 days late x 2 = 12 fine. Ravi is notified; nobody else can borrow it until Ravi does (or the hold lapses). A library with 50,000 titles and 120,000 copies is tiny data, so correctness matters far more than performance.

Industry examples. Koha and Evergreen (open-source library systems), OverDrive/Libby (digital lending with holds queues), university library systems, and the same lending model in equipment rental or Blockbuster-style rentals.

Everyday analogy. A school library card: you can take 3 books, each for two weeks, and if a book is out you can join the waiting list.

Common interview traps.

  • Modelling a book and a physical copy as the same thing (cannot have two copies with different states).
  • Skipping the loan limit and reservations because they are "extra"; they are the interesting rules.
  • Using the real clock so the fine cannot be tested.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• Book (title level): isbn, title, author. Searchable.
  • BookCopy (physical item): copyId, which book, and who has it (null = on shelf).
  • Member: id, name, current loans.
  • Loan: copy, member, due date.
  • FinePolicy (interface): late days to amount.
  • ReservationListener (interface): callback when a reserved title is free.
  • Library: facade holding catalogues, members and waitlists; all rules live here.

The key insight is two-level inventory: a title has many copies; search works on titles, checkout works on copies.

Decision gravity. Splitting Book/BookCopy is a one-way-ish data-model door: merging them later means a schema migration and rewriting every query. Fines and notifications are behind interfaces, which are cheap to change.

Everyday analogy. A bookshop catalogue lists "Harry Potter" once, while the shelf holds five physical copies with different wear.

Common interview traps.

  • Search returning copies instead of titles (duplicate results).
  • Storing the due date on the copy rather than on the loan; history is lost.

notes.title: Class diagram
notes.html:
+----------------------------------------------+
| Library                                      |
| books:     Map<isbn, Book>                   |
| copies:    Map<isbn, List<BookCopy>>         |
| members:   Map<id, Member>                   |
| waitlist:  Map<isbn, Deque<memberId>>        |
| today: Supplier<LocalDate>                   |
| search(q) / checkout(m,isbn) / giveBack(m,c) |
| reserve(m,isbn)                              |
+--+----------+-----------+--------------------+
   |          |           |
   v          v           v
+------+  +----------+  +--------+      <<interface>>
| Book |  | BookCopy |  | Member |      FinePolicy ---- PerDayFine
|isbn  |<-|copyId    |  |loans[] |      fine(daysLate)
|title |  |borrowedBy|  +---+----+
|author|  +----------+      |            <<interface>>
+------+                    v            ReservationListener
                        +------+         onAvailable(member, book)
                        | Loan |
                        |copy, |
                        |member|
                        |due   |
                        +------+

How to read it. Library is a Facade: callers use four methods, and it enforces limit, waitlist order and fines. Money and time policy are injected.

Common interview traps.

  • Splitting rules across Member and Book classes so no single place guarantees "limit 3".
  • Making Library a singleton with static state (untestable). Pass it around.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Facade (Library): one entry point hides catalogue, loans and queue coordination. Why: a small API with all rules in one place. Alternative: separate LoanService, CatalogService, ReservationService (better at larger scale; each can be owned by a team). Reversible.
  • Strategy (FinePolicy): fine formula (flat per day, capped at book price, free for staff) swappable. Why: policy changes often; code should not.
  • Observer (ReservationListener): the library announces "a reserved title is back" without knowing how (email, SMS, push). Reuse the Notification system (P8) behind it.
  • Dependency injection of time (Supplier<LocalDate>): tests can move 20 days forward instantly.
  • FIFO queue (ArrayDeque) per title: fair reservations.

Industry examples. OverDrive "holds" use the same FIFO queue with a "you have 72 hours to borrow" window; hotel and car rental systems use identical title/unit separation (room type vs room).

Everyday analogy. The "Next customer" ticket machine at a bank: first number called, first served.

Common interview traps.

  • Letting anyone borrow a reserved copy because the check only looks at "available".
  • Hardcoding 14, 3 and the fine into methods; at least use named constants.

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
Full runnable file Main.java (catalogue, limit, fines, waitlist and a concurrent checkout test):

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.Supplier;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

/** A title (what you search for) vs a copy (what you physically borrow). Two classes, not one. */
class Book {
    final String isbn, title, author;
    Book(String isbn, String title, String author) { this.isbn = isbn; this.title = title; this.author = author; }
}

class BookCopy {
    final String copyId; final Book book;
    private String borrowedBy;                 // null = on the shelf
    BookCopy(String copyId, Book book) { this.copyId = copyId; this.book = book; }
    boolean isAvailable() { return borrowedBy == null; }
    void borrow(String memberId) { borrowedBy = memberId; }
    void giveBack() { borrowedBy = null; }
}

class Member {
    final String id, name; final List<Loan> loans = new ArrayList<>();
    Member(String id, String name) { this.id = id; this.name = name; }
}

class Loan {
    final BookCopy copy; final Member member; final LocalDate dueDate;
    Loan(BookCopy copy, Member member, LocalDate dueDate) { this.copy = copy; this.member = member; this.dueDate = dueDate; }
}

/** Strategy for fines so policy changes do not touch Library. */
interface FinePolicy { long fine(long daysLate); }
class PerDayFine implements FinePolicy {
    private final long perDay; PerDayFine(long perDay) { this.perDay = perDay; }
    public long fine(long daysLate) { return daysLate <= 0 ? 0 : daysLate * perDay; }
}

/** Observer: told when a reserved title becomes free. */
interface ReservationListener { void onAvailable(String memberId, Book book); }

class Library {
    static final int MAX_LOANS = 3, LOAN_DAYS = 14;
    private final Map<String, Book> books = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, List<BookCopy>> copies = new HashMap<>();       // isbn -> copies
    private final Map<String, Member> members = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Deque<String>> waitlist = new HashMap<>();      // isbn -> queued member ids
    private final Supplier<LocalDate> today; private final FinePolicy fines; private final ReservationListener listener;

    Library(Supplier<LocalDate> today, FinePolicy fines, ReservationListener listener) {
        this.today = today; this.fines = fines; this.listener = listener;
    }
    synchronized void addBook(Book b, int nCopies) {
        books.put(b.isbn, b);
        List<BookCopy> l = copies.computeIfAbsent(b.isbn, k -> new ArrayList<>());
        for (int i = 0; i < nCopies; i++) l.add(new BookCopy(b.isbn + "-" + (l.size() + 1), b));
    }
    synchronized void addMember(Member m) { members.put(m.id, m); }

    synchronized List<Book> search(String q) {
        String s = q.toLowerCase();
        return books.values().stream().filter(b -> b.title.toLowerCase().contains(s) || b.author.toLowerCase().contains(s))
                .sorted(Comparator.comparing(b -> b.title)).collect(Collectors.toList());
    }

    /** Whole check-out is one critical section so two members cannot take the last copy. */
    synchronized Loan checkout(String memberId, String isbn) {
        Member m = members.get(memberId);
        if (m == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown member");
        if (m.loans.size() >= MAX_LOANS) throw new IllegalStateException("loan limit reached");
        Deque<String> q = waitlist.getOrDefault(isbn, new ArrayDeque<>());
        if (!q.isEmpty() && !q.peekFirst().equals(memberId)) throw new IllegalStateException("reserved for someone else");
        BookCopy copy = copies.getOrDefault(isbn, List.of()).stream().filter(BookCopy::isAvailable).findFirst()
                .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalStateException("no copy available"));
        if (!q.isEmpty()) q.pollFirst();
        copy.borrow(memberId);
        Loan loan = new Loan(copy, m, today.get().plusDays(LOAN_DAYS));
        m.loans.add(loan);
        return loan;
    }

    /** Returns the fine owed (0 if on time). */
    synchronized long giveBack(String memberId, String copyId) {
        Member m = members.get(memberId);
        Loan loan = m.loans.stream().filter(l -> l.copy.copyId.equals(copyId)).findFirst()
                .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalStateException("not borrowed by this member"));
        m.loans.remove(loan);
        loan.copy.giveBack();
        long late = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(loan.dueDate, today.get());
        Deque<String> q = waitlist.get(loan.copy.book.isbn);
        if (q != null && !q.isEmpty()) listener.onAvailable(q.peekFirst(), loan.copy.book);
        return fines.fine(late);
    }

    synchronized void reserve(String memberId, String isbn) {
        boolean anyFree = copies.getOrDefault(isbn, List.of()).stream().anyMatch(BookCopy::isAvailable);
        if (anyFree) throw new IllegalStateException("copy is available, just check it out");
        waitlist.computeIfAbsent(isbn, k -> new ArrayDeque<>()).addLast(memberId);
    }
}

public class Main {
    static void check(boolean c, String msg) { if (!c) throw new AssertionError(msg); }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        LocalDate[] day = {LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 1)};
        List<String> notices = new ArrayList<>();
        Library lib = new Library(() -> day[0], new PerDayFine(2), (mid, b) -> notices.add(mid + ":" + b.title));
        lib.addBook(new Book("111", "Clean Code", "Martin"), 1);
        lib.addBook(new Book("222", "Effective Java", "Bloch"), 2);
        lib.addBook(new Book("333", "Refactoring", "Fowler"), 1);
        lib.addBook(new Book("444", "DDIA", "Kleppmann"), 1);
        lib.addMember(new Member("m1", "Asha")); lib.addMember(new Member("m2", "Ravi"));

        check(lib.search("java").size() == 1 && lib.search("MARTIN").size() == 1, "search title/author");
        Loan l = lib.checkout("m1", "111");
        lib.reserve("m2", "111");
        lib.checkout("m1", "222"); lib.checkout("m1", "333");
        boolean limited = false;
        try { lib.checkout("m1", "444"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { limited = true; }
        check(limited, "max 3 loans");

        day[0] = day[0].plusDays(20);                         // 6 days late
        check(lib.giveBack("m1", l.copy.copyId) == 12, "6 days * 2");
        check(notices.equals(List.of("m2:Clean Code")), "waitlist notified");
        boolean blocked = false;
        try { lib.checkout("m1", "111"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { blocked = true; }
        check(blocked, "copy held for m2");
        lib.checkout("m2", "111");

        // concurrency: 2 copies of "222" minus 1 taken = 1 left; 20 members race, exactly one wins
        for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) lib.addMember(new Member("x" + i, "x"));
        java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger won = new java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger();
        Thread[] ts = new Thread[20];
        for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
            final String id = "x" + i;
            ts[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { lib.checkout(id, "222"); won.incrementAndGet(); } catch (IllegalStateException ignored) {} });
            ts[i].start();
        }
        for (Thread t : ts) t.join();
        check(won.get() == 1, "one copy left, winners=" + won.get());
        System.out.println("P12 OK");
    }
}

The core in Kotlin:

import java.time.LocalDate
import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit

class Book(val isbn: String, val title: String, val author: String)
class BookCopy(val copyId: String, val book: Book) { var borrowedBy: String? = null }
class Loan(val copy: BookCopy, val memberId: String, val due: LocalDate)

class Library(private val today: () -> LocalDate,
              private val finePerDay: Long = 2,
              private val onAvailable: (String, Book) -> Unit = { _, _ -> }) {
    private val copies = HashMap<String, MutableList<BookCopy>>()
    private val loans = HashMap<String, MutableList<Loan>>()       // memberId -> loans
    private val waitlist = HashMap<String, ArrayDeque<String>>()   // isbn -> member ids

    @Synchronized fun checkout(memberId: String, isbn: String): Loan {
        val mine = loans.getOrPut(memberId) { mutableListOf() }
        check(mine.size < 3) { "loan limit reached" }
        val q = waitlist[isbn]
        check(q.isNullOrEmpty() || q.first() == memberId) { "reserved for someone else" }
        val copy = copies[isbn].orEmpty().firstOrNull { it.borrowedBy == null }
            ?: error("no copy available")
        q?.removeFirstOrNull()
        copy.borrowedBy = memberId
        return Loan(copy, memberId, today().plusDays(14)).also { mine += it }
    }

    @Synchronized fun giveBack(memberId: String, copyId: String): Long {
        val mine = loans.getValue(memberId)
        val loan = mine.first { it.copy.copyId == copyId }
        mine.remove(loan); loan.copy.borrowedBy = null
        waitlist[loan.copy.book.isbn]?.firstOrNull()?.let { onAvailable(it, loan.copy.book) }
        val late = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(loan.due, today())
        return if (late > 0) late * finePerDay else 0
    }
}

Walk-through. Return on day 21 of a loan due on day 14 gives between(due, today) = 6, times 2 = 12. Returning on day 14 or earlier gives 0 or negative, which the policy maps to 0.

Common interview traps.

  • Computing "days late" with Date arithmetic and time zones; use LocalDate.
  • Notifying the listener while holding internal locks in a way that lets it call back into Library and deadlock (here the lock is reentrant, but production listeners should enqueue instead).
  • Removing the member from the waitlist only on checkout but never expiring stale holds.

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
javac Main.java && java -ea Main
# prints: P12 OK

The test fixes the date to 1 Jan 2026 and moves it. It asserts: case-insensitive search by title and author; the fourth concurrent loan is refused (limit 3); returning 6 days late costs 12; the waitlisted member is notified and another member's checkout is blocked while the copy is held; and 20 threads racing for the last copy of a title produce exactly one winner.

Common interview traps.

  • No negative test (limit exceeded, copy unavailable). The error paths are the rules.
  • Forgetting to test "return a book you did not borrow".

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
Race to avoid: two members call checkout for the last copy at the same moment. Both see isAvailable() true, both mark it borrowed, and one copy ends up loaned twice. Same for the member limit: two simultaneous checkouts could both pass loans.size() < 3.

  • Shown: every state-changing method on Library is synchronized. The check (limit, waitlist, availability) and the update (mark borrowed, add loan) are one atomic step. The 20-thread test yields exactly one winner. For a library with perhaps 1 to 10 checkouts per second, a single lock is more than enough.
  • Finer-grained: lock per ISBN for copy assignment, plus per-member lock for the limit, always taken in a fixed order (member id then isbn) to avoid deadlock. Needed only at very high contention, which a library will never see.
  • Database version: UPDATE copy SET borrowed_by=? WHERE copy_id=? AND borrowed_by IS NULL and check rows affected; a unique partial index on (copy_id) WHERE returned_at IS NULL on the loans table makes double-loan impossible even with bugs. Member limit: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the member row, or a constraint trigger.
  • Reads (search) can use a snapshot or cache without the write lock; the catalogue changes rarely.

Incident pattern. Duplicate loans appear after a retry: the mobile app times out, the user taps again, two loans created. Symptom: member shows 2 loans for the same copy. Fix: idempotency key per checkout request, plus the unique index.

Decision gravity. A coarse lock is the correct first choice: reversible, simple, and impossible to deadlock. Do not optimise concurrency in a system whose peak is a few requests a second.

Everyday analogy. One librarian at the desk handles one person at a time, so the last copy cannot be handed to two people.

Common interview traps.

  • Locking on the Book object rather than on the shared inventory (different Book instances for the same isbn).
  • Checking availability in one synchronized method and loaning in another (check-then-act gap).

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Renewals: extend the due date once, only if no one is waitlisted.
  • Reservation expiry: if the head of the waitlist does not borrow within 3 days, move to the next (scheduled job or lazy check).
  • Lost / damaged copy: copy state LOST with a replacement fee.
  • Roles: librarian adds books, members borrow; permissions.
  • Search at scale: inverted index or Elasticsearch / Postgres full-text instead of scanning (search here is O(n) over titles).
  • Branches: copies have a branchId; inter-branch transfers.
  • Digital lending: copies are licences; same hold queue, different limits.
  • Notifications: due-soon and overdue reminders through the Notification system (P8).

Common interview traps.

  • Linear search presented as production-ready; say what you would index.
  • Letting fines accumulate unbounded; cap at the book price or block borrowing above a threshold.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Two-level model: Book (title, searchable) and BookCopy (physical, borrowable); loans record due date.
  • Library is a facade enforcing limit, FIFO reservations and fines; fine policy and notifications are injected (Strategy, Observer).
  • Inject the clock so late-fee logic is testable.
  • Make check-and-update atomic (synchronized here, conditional SQL update plus unique index in a database).
  • Extensions: renewals, reservation expiry, branches, search index, reminders.

questions.promptHtml: Why model Book and BookCopy as two classes in a library system?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the first modelling decision; getting it wrong breaks search, loans and reservations at once.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A book is a title (ISBN, author) that people search for; a copy is a physical item that one person borrows. A title can have five copies in different states. If they are one class, I cannot say "2 of 5 copies are out", cannot track who holds which copy, and search returns duplicates. So search works on titles, checkout works on copies, and the loan (not the copy) stores the due date.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Two-level inventory: Book (isbn) 1 -> * BookCopy. Availability of a title = any copy with borrowedBy == null.
  • Loan(copy, member, due) is a separate object so history is kept; due date on the copy would be overwritten on the next loan.
  • Same pattern as room type vs room in hotels or SKU vs unit in warehouses.
Book(isbn 111) -> Copy 111-1 (on shelf)
               -> Copy 111-2 (loan: Asha, due 15 Jan)
               -> Copy 111-3 (lost)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Search returning copies, so a title appears five times.
  • Putting dueDate on the copy and losing loan history.
  • Different Book objects for the same ISBN so locks and equality disagree.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do reservations attach? -> To the title (ISBN): the first free copy goes to the head of the queue.
  2. What changes for digital lending? -> Copies become licences with a limited count; same hold queue.
  3. What is the one-way door? -> The data model split: merging later means a schema migration and query rewrite.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "a book has a count of available copies". Senior: model copies as entities with state (shelf, loaned, lost, damaged), and explain why a counter hides who holds what and breaks with returns of lost copies.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A system stored only available_count per title; an audit found 300 books "available" that were actually lost, and nobody could tell which.

questions.contextHtml:
A reviewer finds two problems in checkout: members sometimes borrow a copy that was reserved for someone else, and in tests two members occasionally both get the last copy. Code:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
boolean available(String isbn) {
    return copies.get(isbn).stream().anyMatch(BookCopy::isAvailable);
}

Loan checkout(String memberId, String isbn) {
    if (!available(isbn)) throw new IllegalStateException("none");
    return doCheckout(memberId, isbn);          // not synchronized
}

private synchronized Loan doCheckout(String memberId, String isbn) {
    Member m = members.get(memberId);
    BookCopy c = copies.get(isbn).stream().filter(BookCopy::isAvailable).findFirst().get();
    c.borrow(memberId);
    Loan l = new Loan(c, m, today.get().plusDays(14));
    m.loans.add(l);
    return l;
}
fun available(isbn: String) = copies.getValue(isbn).any { it.borrowedBy == null }

fun checkout(memberId: String, isbn: String): Loan {
    check(available(isbn)) { "none" }
    return doCheckout(memberId, isbn)
}

@Synchronized private fun doCheckout(memberId: String, isbn: String): Loan {
    val c = copies.getValue(isbn).first { it.borrowedBy == null }
    c.borrowedBy = memberId
    return Loan(c, memberId, today().plusDays(14)).also { loans.getOrPut(memberId) { mutableListOf() } += it }
}
questions.promptHtml: List every defect and give the corrected method.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Says "add synchronized to checkout" and nothing else, missing the missing loan-limit and waitlist rules.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What are the rules: max 3 loans, FIFO reservations? Which lock protects the inventory?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (review), but I would block the merge: duplicate loans are a data integrity bug.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Check-then-act gap: available is checked outside the lock, then doCheckout runs, so two threads can both pass the check; inside, findFirst().get() throws NoSuchElementException for the loser, or both take the same copy if the check races. (b) Waitlist ignored: availability only looks at copies, so a reserved copy is lent to anyone. (c) Loan limit (3) is never enforced. (d) get() on an Optional gives a poor error.
  4. How I'd verify: The 20-thread test with one copy left must yield exactly one winner and the others a clean IllegalStateException; a test for "reserved for someone else"; a test for the fourth loan.
  5. Root cause: Rules and the state change are not one critical section.
  6. Fix: Put all checks (member, limit, waitlist head, copy availability) and the update inside one synchronized method, as in the reference code, and poll the waitlist head only when the borrower is that head.
  7. Prevention: Negative tests for every rule; a lint/review rule: "never check state in one method and mutate in another."
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: One coarse lock is right for a library (1 to 10 checkouts per second); I would not introduce per-ISBN locks first.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Locking on the Book object? -> Wrong: different Book instances can share an ISBN; lock the shared Library or an ISBN-keyed lock map.
  • The listener is called inside the lock? -> Reentrant here, but production listeners should enqueue, not call back in.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite where a split check/act design handed one copy to two patrons on a Saturday morning and the front desk found out by fistfight.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only adds synchronized somewhere.
  • Hire: finds the check-then-act gap, the missing waitlist and limit checks.
  • Strong hire: also fixes error handling, explains lock choice and writes the race test.

questions.contextHtml: Product adds two rules: (1) when a reserved book comes back, the head of the waitlist has 3 days to borrow it, otherwise it moves to the next member; (2) members may renew a loan once for 14 days, but only if nobody is waiting. Today giveBack calls the listener immediately and checkout blocks others only while the queue is non-empty. No scheduler exists in the code base.
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change, how do you implement expiry without a thread per reservation, and what edge cases do you test?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Starts a Thread.sleep(3 days) per reservation, or adds renewal flags on Member.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the held copy stay off the shelf for others? What if the head has hit the loan limit? Is "3 days" calendar or library days? Renewal count per loan or per member?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; design decision.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Options: scheduled job sweeping expired holds; or lazy expiry (check heldUntil on every access). Lazy is simplest and testable with the injected clock; a sweeper is needed only to send "your hold expired" notices.
  4. How I'd verify: Fake today: return on day 1, advance 4 days, next member's checkout succeeds and the first member's hold is gone.
  5. Root cause / design: Add Hold(memberId, heldUntil) to the head of the waitlist and a renewedOnce flag on Loan (state belongs to the loan). checkout first drops expired holds. renew(memberId, copyId) throws if the waitlist for that ISBN is non-empty or already renewed. Library stays the facade; no change to Book, BookCopy, FinePolicy.
  6. Fix: Java and Kotlin sketch:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
synchronized void renew(String memberId, String copyId) {
    Loan l = findLoan(memberId, copyId);
    if (l.renewed) throw new IllegalStateException("already renewed");
    Deque<Hold> q = waitlist.get(l.copy.book.isbn);
    if (q != null && !q.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("someone is waiting");
    l.dueDate = l.dueDate.plusDays(LOAN_DAYS); l.renewed = true;   // dueDate no longer final
}
@Synchronized fun renew(memberId: String, copyId: String) {
    val l = findLoan(memberId, copyId)
    check(!l.renewed) { "already renewed" }
    check(waitlist[l.copy.book.isbn].isNullOrEmpty()) { "someone is waiting" }
    l.due = l.due.plusDays(14); l.renewed = true
}
  1. Prevention: Tests: hold expiry boundary (day 3 vs day 4), renewal when queue empty vs not, renewal twice, expired hold promotes next, hold skipped for a member at the loan limit.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not spawn a timer per reservation (thousands of sleeping threads, lost on restart). Lazy expiry plus one daily sweeper job for notices is cheap and survives restarts if holds are persisted.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Sweeper and checkout both expire the same hold? -> Both run under the same lock or use a conditional update in SQL.
  • Hold window per branch? -> Policy object chosen per branch, same Strategy idea as FinePolicy.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite where reservations "expired" only when a nightly job ran, so for 20 hours each night a ghost hold blocked a popular title.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: thread-per-reservation.
  • Hire: lazy expiry with injected clock, flag on the loan, correct classes.
  • Strong hire: edge cases (head at limit, boundaries), sweeper only for notices, persistence and idempotent expiry.

questions.contextHtml: The library moved to a Postgres-backed service with two app servers. Support reports members with two loans for the same copy: loans has rows (copy 222-1, member m17) twice, created 1.4 seconds apart. Mobile app logs show a request timeout at 1,000 ms followed by an automatic retry. Server CPU is 12%; database p99 is 40 ms. Another engineer suspects a bug in the fine calculation.
questions.promptHtml: Find the cause and make double-loan impossible even if the application has bugs.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds an in-JVM synchronized which does nothing across two servers, or increases the client timeout only.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the first request succeed after the client gave up? Is there a unique constraint on active loans? Do both rows have different request ids? Which isolation level?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Delete or mark the duplicates (soft-void), and temporarily raise the mobile timeout to 5 s to stop retries storming.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Retry after a slow-but-successful first call: classic duplicate submit (fits the 1.4 s gap). (b) Two servers racing with no DB constraint. (c) Fine logic: a red herring, unrelated to loans.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare request ids/timestamps, check loans indexes with \d loans, replay the call twice in a test.
  5. Root cause: Non-idempotent checkout, and invariants enforced only in application memory.
  6. Fix: Add a partial unique index so one active loan per copy: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_active_loan ON loans(copy_id) WHERE returned_at IS NULL; Claim the copy atomically: UPDATE copy SET borrowed_by=? WHERE copy_id=? AND borrowed_by IS NULL and check rows affected = 1. Add an idempotency key per checkout request (client generates UUID, unique column), so the retry returns the same loan.
  7. Prevention: A concurrency test against the real DB, an idempotency contract for all mutating endpoints, an alert on constraint violations.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not rely on synchronized (per JVM) and not use SERIALIZABLE globally just for this; the constraint plus idempotency key is cheaper and visible.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Member limit of 3 with two servers? -> SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the member row, or a constraint trigger.
  • Idempotency key reused with different payload? -> Reject with 422 or 409.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite where a double-tap on a flaky network created duplicates for months until a constraint made the bug loud on day one.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: JVM lock.
  • Hire: partial unique index plus conditional update.
  • Strong hire: adds idempotency key, member-row locking, monitoring and the cheap-over-serializable trade-off.

questions.contextHtml: search(q) streams all titles, lowercases and does contains. It was fine for 50,000 titles. The library network is merging with a consortium: 5 million titles, 800 searches per second at peak, p99 budget 100 ms. Today profiling shows 3 s per search at 5M titles and a CPU pegged at 100%. The Library search holds the same lock as checkout, and checkouts now time out.
questions.promptHtml: How do you redesign search and decouple it from the write path?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds a cache for query strings; misses that scan cost and lock contention are the real problems.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Exact title, prefix, fuzzy or author? Freshness requirement (is 5 s stale OK)? Do we need ranking? Is the catalogue mostly read-only?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move search off the Library lock immediately (read from an immutable snapshot) so checkouts recover; add a 100 ms timeout.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) O(n) scan x 800 qps = 4 billion title checks per second: impossible. (b) Shared lock: search starves writes. (c) String allocations from toLowerCase per title: secondary cost.
  4. How I'd verify: Flame graph (async-profiler), lock hold metrics, and a microbenchmark of the scan.
  5. Root cause: Algorithm O(n) per query and one coarse lock for reads and writes.
  6. Fix: An inverted index (token to ISBN list) or Postgres full-text (GIN index) or Elasticsearch; build it from the catalogue and update on addBook. Reads use a copy-on-write snapshot, so no lock; staleness of a few seconds is fine because catalogues change rarely. Availability is displayed from a separate fast lookup, not from the index.
  7. Prevention: Load test at 2x peak, p99 SLO alert, a rule that read paths never take write locks.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: An external search cluster adds ops cost; Postgres FTS covers 5M titles with an tsvector GIN index (verify latency on your data). I would not add an LRU cache on query strings first.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Typos? -> Trigram index (pg_trgm) or fuzzy match in the search engine.
  • Index shows "available" but copy was just taken? -> Treat availability as a hint and re-check on checkout.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident where a "harmless" admin catalogue search shared a lock with checkout and caused a morning outage.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: query cache.
  • Hire: inverted index or FTS and lock separation.
  • Strong hire: staleness trade-off, availability as a hint, SLO test and index cost.

questions.contextHtml: giveBack calls listener.onAvailable(...) while holding the Library lock. The production listener sends an email through an SMTP gateway that, on Friday, takes 6 seconds per call. Return desks now freeze: p99 of giveBack is 9 s; thread dump shows 40 threads waiting on the Library monitor and one inside SmtpListener.send. Another engineer proposes "make the lock fair".
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure, fix it, and say what you trade.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Tunes lock fairness or adds a longer SMTP timeout.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is notification required to happen before the return completes? Is loss acceptable (retry)? Throughput of returns?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make the listener a no-op or enqueue to an in-memory queue; return desks recover.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Slow I/O while holding the global lock serializes everything. (b) A listener that calls back into Library could deadlock or reenter: second-order risk. (c) Lock fairness is irrelevant.
  4. How I'd verify: jstack showing the owner of the monitor in Smtp..., lock-wait time metric.
  5. Root cause: Calling an untrusted slow collaborator inside a critical section.
  6. Fix: Collect the notification inside the lock, publish after releasing: return an event, or drop it in an ExecutorService/queue. Persist notifications (outbox table) so a crash does not lose them; the worker retries with backoff.
  7. Prevention: Review rule "no I/O, no callbacks inside locks"; timeout on all external calls; metric for lock hold time.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Async notification can be delayed or duplicated; make the consumer idempotent. I would not hold the lock to guarantee ordering of emails: order does not matter for "your book is ready".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Email fails permanently? -> Dead-letter queue and a "notify failed" counter; the hold remains valid.
  • Need exactly-once? -> Not realistic; at-least-once with idempotent send keyed by (member, isbn, hold id).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident where one slow email provider froze checkout across 30 branches because the notifier ran inside the inventory lock.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes the lock.
  • Hire: moves notification outside the lock via queue.
  • Strong hire: outbox, idempotency, retry/DLQ and the I/O-under-lock review rule.

questions.promptHtml: How do you design the fine calculation so it can be tested for a book returned 6 days late?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Time and money rules are where code reviews find real bugs; the question tests dependency injection and policy separation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I inject the date as a Supplier<LocalDate> and the fine formula as a FinePolicy strategy. In the test I fix today to 1 Jan, check out, move the date forward 20 days, return, and assert 6 days x 2 = 12. A PerDayFine returns 0 for zero or negative late days. No sleeping, no time zones, and policy changes (capped fine, staff exempt) do not touch Library.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(dueDate, today) on LocalDate gives 6 for a loan taken 1 Jan (due 15 Jan) and returned 21 Jan.
  • Money as long minor units, never double.
  • Boundary tests: returned on due date (0), one day late (2), early (negative becomes 0).
loan day 1 -> due day 15 -> return day 21 -> late 6 -> fine 12

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface FinePolicy { long fine(long daysLate); }
class PerDayFine implements FinePolicy {
    private final long perDay; PerDayFine(long p) { perDay = p; }
    public long fine(long late) { return late <= 0 ? 0 : late * perDay; }
}
fun interface FinePolicy { fun fine(daysLate: Long): Long }
class PerDayFine(private val perDay: Long) : FinePolicy {
    override fun fine(daysLate: Long) = if (daysLate <= 0) 0 else daysLate * perDay
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• new Date() inside the method, so tests depend on the real day.
  • double for money.
  • No test for returning early or on the due date.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Fine capped at the book price? -> New CappedFine policy wrapping PerDayFine; Library unchanged.
  2. Fines unpaid, block borrowing? -> A check in checkout against member.outstanding; add a threshold constant or policy.
  3. Time zones? -> LocalDate in the library's zone; pass a Clock with a zone if branches span zones.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use Date.getTime() difference". Senior: injects time, uses LocalDate, separates policy, adds boundary tests and caps unbounded fines.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A system calculated fines using server time in UTC while the library closed at midnight IST, so books returned at 11 pm were fined a day.

questions.contextHtml: The single-branch in-memory Library (one synchronized lock) must become a 12-branch service backed by Postgres, with inter-branch transfers, without downtime. Peak is 60 checkouts per second across branches (not per branch). A pilot with two app servers showed double loans within a day. The business refuses a read-only window longer than 5 minutes. Existing data: 3M copies, 1.2M active loans.
questions.promptHtml: Plan the migration and the concurrency strategy. What is reversible and what is a one-way door?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Take the system down at night and copy the data", or keep a JVM lock and run several servers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can members be tied to one home branch? Is eventual consistency acceptable for search? How are copies identified across branches? What is the rollback plan?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the double loans in the pilot: add the unique index and conditional update first, even before the migration.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Risks: (a) invariants live only in JVM memory; (b) dual write inconsistency during cutover; (c) hot rows for popular titles (red herring at 60 req/s).
  4. How I'd verify: Shadow-read comparison (old vs new answers), counts of loans per member, constraint-violation metrics.
  5. Root cause / design: Add branch_id to copies; invariants move to the DB: UNIQUE (copy_id) WHERE returned_at IS NULL, conditional UPDATE for claiming a copy, FOR UPDATE on the member row for the loan limit. Per-ISBN waitlist ordering with ORDER BY created_at, claim head via SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
  6. Fix (plan): Phase 1: backfill into Postgres while the old system serves writes; Phase 2: dual write with the old system as source of truth and compare; Phase 3: flip reads, then writes behind a flag, branch by branch; Phase 4: retire. Reversible until phase 3; the one-way door is when writes go only to the DB and the old store is no longer updated.
  7. Prevention: Per-branch feature flag, reconciliation job, idempotency keys, dashboards of conflict rates.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use a distributed lock service for each checkout (60 req/s does not justify it) and would not shard by branch yet: one Postgres handles this load.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Transfer between branches loses a copy mid-flight? -> A IN_TRANSIT copy state with a destination, transitions by conditional updates.
  • Two branches both claim the head of a waitlist? -> SKIP LOCKED ensures one claim.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite migration where dual writes without reconciliation silently diverged for two weeks, found only by a patron's complaint.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: big-bang downtime copy, JVM locks.
  • Hire: DB constraints, conditional updates, phased cutover.
  • Strong hire: flag per branch, reconciliation, SKIP LOCKED for waitlist, in-transit state, one-way-door framing.
